claim: ISM-based dependency analysis places four risks -- Injection Attacks, Code Quality and Logic Errors, Backdoors and Malicious Code, and Insufficient Input Validation -- at the top (root) dependency level, meaning these compound into higher-level AI-model and operational risks such as adversarial attacks on AI models and inadequate logging/monitoring.
stance_target: prioritizing automated code-quality/injection/input-validation checks as the foundational layer of an AI software factory's security sweep, since downstream AI-model risks depend on them
scope_conditions: Hybrid ANN-ISM framework case study, generative AI code generation, 2025
quoted_support: At the highest level of the figure, Level 1, four bad risks exist: Injection Attacks, Code Quality and Logic Errors, Backdoors and Malicious Code, and Insufficient Input Validation. These risks stem from the quality and security of the generated code, and their combinations with each other show that if the code quality is bad, or it is not appropriately validated, security threats could enter the code path.

claim: Small software companies show the highest vulnerability to injection attacks, code quality/logic errors, backdoors, and insufficient input validation in automatic code generation, attributed to under-resourced security mechanisms, informal QA processes, and poor control over third-party libraries; larger companies show markedly lower risk-impact percentages due to bigger security budgets and established procedures.
stance_target: designing the software factory's automated security sweep to be especially rigorous for small/under-resourced deployment contexts, since larger orgs' existing defenses do not generalize
scope_conditions: survey-based firm-size analysis across companies using automatic code generation, 2025
quoted_support: Small companies were found to be the most vulnerable to security problems that arise with automatic code generation: they lack funds, knowledge, and protective mechanisms... larger companies, on the other hand, usually have less sweeping effects overall, due to bigger security tools budgets, more well-prepared personnel, and grander schemes of security procedures.

claim: Asia shows the highest regional exposure to Injection Attacks, Backdoors/Malicious Code, and Adversarial Attacks on AI Models among automatic-code-generation cybersecurity risks, attributed to rapid AI adoption outpacing cybersecurity-defense maturity and an uneven regional technology gap; Africa also records elevated impact.
stance_target: regional/deployment-context variation in cybersecurity risk exposure relevant to where a software factory's agents are deployed or trained
scope_conditions: survey-based regional analysis (North America, Europe, Asia, Africa, South America, Oceania), 2025
quoted_support: Asia has the highest exposure to cybersecurity risk vectors, including Injection Attacks, Backdoors, Malicious Code, and Adversarial Attacks on AI Models... This increased impact is the result of the rapid implementation of AI without well-established cybersecurity defenses; in addition, there is a vast technology gap between the various countries in Asia.

claim: A case study at an AI-based code-generation company found the Hybrid ANN-ISM framework effectively handles the primary cybersecurity challenges of injection attacks, code quality, backdoors, and lack of input validation, with static code analysis, automated penetration testing, and adversarial training identified as the highest-promise mitigation techniques.
stance_target: validating a structured risk-mitigation framework (combining predictive ML risk scoring with dependency-structured mitigation) as practical for real-world AI code-generation security management
scope_conditions: single case study, one AI-based code-generation company, 2025
quoted_support: The case study results show that the framework efficiently handles the primary cybersecurity challenges, such as injection attacks, code quality, backdoors, and lack of input validation... techniques such as static code analysis, automated penetration testing, and adversarial training hold much promise.

claim: Black-box deep-learning/LLM code generators are inherently opaque, making it difficult for developers to verify whether AI-generated code follows secure coding principles or conceals vulnerabilities -- an acknowledged limitation motivating structured external risk-mitigation frameworks rather than trusting generator-internal safety.
stance_target: relying on the code-generating model's own outputs/explanations as sufficient evidence of secure code, without external static/dynamic verification
scope_conditions: general property of black-box LLM/deep-learning code generators, as of 2025 literature review
quoted_support: Black-box models like deep neural networks and large language models (LLMs) of the code in code generation risk generating exploitative output without recognizing how individual vulnerabilities or design flaws are being injected into the code. This lack of interpretability makes it challenging for developers to consider if the AI-created code follows the secure coding principles or contains concealed vulnerabilities.

claim: The paper's own stated limitation is that more research is required to improve the scalability, privacy-preservation, and dynamic integration of the ANN-ISM framework with cybersecurity threat intelligence -- real-time/continuous threat-intelligence integration is an explicitly acknowledged gap, not a solved problem.
stance_target: documented absence: continuous/real-time threat-intelligence integration for automated code-generation security frameworks remains an open research gap as of this 2025 paper
scope_conditions: stated limitation/future-work section of the paper, 2025
quoted_support: More research is required to improve the scalability, privacy preserving, and dynamic integration of the framework with cybersecurity threat intelligence.
